omni.title: The next carrier platform needs more than passings.
omni.lede: Omni already incorporates Lit Fiber. The opportunity is to package a credible development engine, municipal relationships and qualified incremental markets for a carrier, while proving the property-level MDU economics.
omni.decision: Lead with delivery capability and incremental market access. Treat the MDU thesis as a potentially valuable differentiator that still needs a property and unit inventory.

angles.title: A development platform for carrier diligence
angles.case: Pair local construction and market development with national retail distribution. Package completed availability, customer cohorts and a funded backlog separately so the carrier can value time-to-market and future growth without paying equally for every stage.
angles.countercase: Existing carrier JVs compete for capital. Distinct geography and repeatable unit economics matter more than another sponsor-backed footprint.
proof: Monthly ready-for-service additions on a consistent perimeter
Cohort take rates and fully loaded completion capex
Carrier-specific incremental addresses and customer transfer economics

angles.title: An MDU capability that can be quantified
angles.case: Create a property-level package showing executed access, contracted units, connected units, wiring rights and installation economics. If that evidence demonstrates a repeatable access advantage, it can make a more persuasive carrier story than a general claim of density.
angles.countercase: A blank access agreement and apartment-rich counties do not establish a large MDU franchise. Bulk contracts may improve acquisition economics while introducing property concentration and renewal risk.
proof: Executed property agreements and assignment rights
Units passed, activated and paying by property
Bulk versus retail economics, churn and common-area capital

angles.title: Lit’s municipal development model
angles.case: Use Medina and Brownsville to demonstrate experience aligning public middle-mile assets with private last-mile delivery. Offer a repeatable process for cities and carriers, supported by the actual contract perimeter.
angles.countercase: Municipal access, ownership and operating obligations can constrain pricing, assignment and exit. Advisory projects are not automatically owned networks or exclusive pipeline.
proof: Legal entity and municipal contract schedule
Ownership of middle mile, last mile and equipment
Operating term, renewals, revenue rights and service obligations

angles.title: A segmented geography story
angles.verdict: Use market clusters, not an affluent average
angles.case: Western Pennsylvania offers an announced integration and expansion narrative around Citizens and Omni’s county plan, with the final Citizens regulatory close still unresolved. Ohio contains both higher-income and lower-income markets; Brownsville and Michigan deserve distinct affordability, construction and adoption cases.
angles.countercase: County or block-group demographics describe places, not actual customer income. A weighted average of local medians is not the footprint’s median household income.
proof: Comparable ACS context with match rates and margins of error
Actual ARPU, affordability, conversion and competitive pricing

facts.title: One operating-platform story
facts.text: Omni and Lit Fiber announced their merger in November 2024. Both were majority-owned by Oak Hill; Stephens and The Pritzker Organization remained shareholders. Current ownership percentages and every transferred contract are not disclosed.

facts.title: Citizens is an announced Pennsylvania expansion
facts.text: Omni announced the Citizens Fiber acquisition in June 2026. A July 11 Pennsylvania notice subsequently sought transfer-of-control approval; final regulatory close has not been verified. The separate plan for nearly 200,000 additional locations across six counties is future construction, not acquired passings.

facts.title: Historical targets are not achieved builds
facts.text: The 2024 and 2025 year-end location figures were targets. Stonepeak later reported 110,000 homes passed as of December 2024, with a perimeter that is not demonstrably identical to the 200,000-location target. This is a reconciliation question, not a proven 90,000-location shortfall. FCC filing changes and acquisitions cannot establish organic construction pace without a consistent bridge.

facts.title: Financing categories remain separate
facts.text: Sponsor commitments, debt financing, equity, working-capital capacity and cumulative deployed capital describe different things. They should not be summed into a single capital-raised or acquisition-capacity number.

facts.title: Operating rights and maintenance have different terms
facts.text: Brownsville discloses an initial five-year operating agreement and a separate 20-year maintenance agreement, each with up to three ten-year renewal options. Renewal control and conditions are not established by the financial-report summary. Optional renewal is not secured revenue duration.

facts.title: Municipal economics must be deducted
facts.text: The FY2025 city report records $61,995 of middle-mile user fees. A July 2026 city update separately describes per-customer revenue sharing with Omni. These disclosures do not establish Omni retained revenue, EBITDA or a recurring run rate.

questions: Address-level overlap with Metronet, Lumos, pending GoNetspeed/Greenlight and i3 perimeters
Existing retail customers versus premises and construction backlog

killTests.evidence_needed: Property-level executed access agreements, contracted and activated units, wiring ownership, contract term/termination and assignability, bulk versus retail terms, installation cost, churn and net revenue by cohort.
killTests.falsifier: A marketing page or a high multifamily share without controlled property access, activated units or differentiated economics.

killTests.evidence_needed: Monthly ready-for-service addresses, gross and net additions, consistent acquisition perimeter, cost-to-complete, cohort take rates, repeatable contractor capacity and service quality.
killTests.falsifier: Counting announced towns, acquired locations or changed FCC reporting as organically completed construction.

killTests.hypothesis: High household income improves carrier attractiveness
killTests.evidence_needed: Address/BG context and actual customer affordability, ARPU, conversion, churn and competitive pricing. Segment markets instead of averaging away variation.
killTests.falsifier: County medians represented as the median income of served households, or an affluent Ohio cluster used to characterize the entire footprint.

killTests.hypothesis: More passings means a better bolt-on
killTests.evidence_needed: Incremental available locations, economic route adjacency, customer cohorts, integration cost, ownership willingness and funded capex obligations.
killTests.falsifier: A large overlapping network, a closed acquisition, or a member-owned/municipal system presented as a readily purchasable independent operator.

timeline.title: Oak Hill forms Omni and commits $250 million from Fund VI
timeline.text: committed equity capital; funded and deployed amounts not disclosed. No actual passings disclosed; management referred prospectively to hundreds of thousands of households. Perimeter: Omni Fiber initial Ohio, Pennsylvania, and Michigan plan

timeline.title: Oak Hill commits $150 million of primary capital to Lit and becomes majority investor
timeline.text: committed primary equity; funded and deployed amounts not disclosed. Approximately 20,000 homes and businesses reached actual; more than 200,000 locations over the next few years target. Perimeter: Lit Communities; Stephens, TPO, and management remain shareholders

timeline.title: Omni closes $150 million Stonepeak Credit debt financing
timeline.text: closed term-debt financing. More than $250 million invested actual; over 25 communities served and over 15 under construction actual; approximately 200,000 locations by year-end 2024 target. Perimeter: Pre-Lit-merger Omni

timeline.title: Omni and Lit announce merger
timeline.text: merger announced; complete legal terms and exact close date not disclosed. Network and systems integration in early 2025 target. Perimeter: Lit Fiber operating footprint in Medina County and Brownsville disclosed; broader Lit Communities contract perimeter not enumerated

timeline.title: Stonepeak lender presentation measurement date
timeline.text: lender-reported actual-type operating metric. 110,000 homes passed in less than two years. Perimeter: Slide describes Omni in Ohio, Michigan, and Pennsylvania; Lit/Texas inclusion not established

timeline.title: Brownsville officially launches Omni-branded retail service
timeline.text: customer-facing brand and service launch. No completed-location count disclosed. Perimeter: Brownsville, Texas

timeline.title: Brownsville FY2025 report recognizes Omni as surviving Lit merger entity
timeline.text: government corroboration of completed corporate reorganization by fiscal year-end. No systemwide integration completion or location count disclosed. Perimeter: Brownsville Lit/Omni municipal contracts; obligations unchanged and counterparty name updated

timeline.title: Omni closes $150 million incremental debt, $50 million incremental Oak Hill equity, and separate $10 million working-capital facility
timeline.text: closed financing; debt draw status not fully disclosed. More than $400 million invested actual; approximately 60 communities served and 25 under construction actual; approximately 340,000 locations by year-end 2025 target. Perimeter: Post-Lit-merger Omni across Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan, and Texas

timeline.title: SEC-filed OHA fund holdings show Omni first-lien loans and an incremental delayed-draw commitment
timeline.text: fund-level holding evidence; not companywide debt balance. Not applicable; filing confirms an unfunded portion of that fund's delayed-draw commitment. Perimeter: One OHA-managed fund's slice of Omni debt

timeline.title: Omni announces Citizens acquisition and transition
timeline.text: company-announced acquisition; regulatory close not established. More than $500 million invested in construction actual on Omni's then-stated perimeter; nearly 200,000 additional western Pennsylvania locations target. Perimeter: Citizens Westmoreland County operations; price, subscribers, passings, route miles, and EBITDA undisclosed

timeline.title: Pennsylvania publishes Citizens transfer-of-control application notice
timeline.text: regulatory application pending at notice date; protests due 2026-07-27. No operating scale disclosed. Perimeter: Omni plus three named Citizens legal entities

timeline.title: Current operating-page check
timeline.text: Citizens retains a standalone consumer site, support, bill-pay, and brand; Omni lists some western Pennsylvania markets as available, partial, or coming soon. No companywide actual passings, ready-for-service locations, or subscriber count disclosed. Perimeter: Marketing and customer-operation status only; not legal close proof

measuredContext.methodology: Join 12-digit block-group GEOIDs from D25 FTTP residential-capable locations to 2020-2024 ACS block-group estimates. Weight each block-group metric by the filer's unique reported R/X availability locations in that block group. Income uses 2024 inflation-adjusted dollars. Open-ended income endpoints identified by ACS MOE sentinel -333333333 are excluded from ordinary averages and income bins. No customer-level demographic data are used.
measuredContext.interpretation: Income is an availability-location-weighted average of reported closed-interval block-group median household incomes, not the median income of the footprint or customers. Apartment share uses all housing units, including vacant units. Renter share uses occupied housing units. An FCC location can represent an entire multi-unit building, so these weights can underrepresent units in those buildings.
measuredContext.perimeter: Omni filer 480067 and Citizens/Kecksburg filer 130264 (announced Omni acquisition; final regulatory close unresolved) remain separate rows. No cross-filer union is claimed. Lit Fiber filer 450069 is a distinct legal-filer identity requiring resolution before joining to the acquired Lit business.
measuredContext.geography: FCC-reported 2020 block geography joined by identical 12-digit GEOID to ACS 2024 publication geography; match rates are disclosed. Missing or open-ended income estimates are excluded metric by metric, not set to zero.
measuredContext.uncertainty: ACS income estimates are in 2024 dollars and have 90% margins of error. A combined margin of error is not computed; weighted values are descriptive context, not statistically ranked income estimates.

acceleratedAnalyses.title: Omni / Lit: prove the MDU economics property by property
acceleratedAnalyses.summary: Omni has a documented MDU sales and access process, plus one qualified property-manager listing that markets fiber availability. The reviewed public record does not yet establish a signed MDU portfolio, a bulk-contract base or superior property economics. The pitch should make those claims conditional on the property book. [M01] [M02] [M03]
acceleratedAnalyses.scope: Omni and integrated Lit operations are the subject of this analysis. Socket and IdeaTek remain a separate sponsor-platform case. A property listing, blank agreement or municipal right-of-way is not a verified contract, installed-unit schedule or customer base.

platform.name: Rightfiber (Ritter Communications + Great Plains Communications)
platform.facility_purpose: Continued organic growth and potential M&A
platform.capital_limitation: Facility size is not cash available, undrawn headroom, debt outstanding or acquisition capacity. Drawn balance, covenants, committed capex and liquidity remain unknown.
platform.scope_limitation: 20-state combined network reach is not a 20-state residential FTTH footprint. Legacy filers remain separate in historical FCC data until a supported current grouping is applied.

carriers.name: T-Mobile

public_facts.claim: Announced a 50/50 Oak Hill JV for GoNetspeed and Greenlight; expected investment approximately $2.0 billion for a half interest and substantially all existing residential fiber customers. Expected closing 1H 2027 in the announcement.

Existing Metronet JV closed July 24, 2025; T-Mobile's 2025 filing records $4.6 billion invested for a half interest and 713,000 residential fiber customers. Metronet transitioned to a wholesale model.

carriers.pitch_inference: Offer a distinct market-and-execution package: qualified incremental addresses, proven construction cohorts, transferable MDU access rights and a wholesale operating model. Oak Hill's existing relationship can reduce introduction friction, but does not establish appetite for another transaction.
carriers.best_structure_hypothesis: Selected-market wholesale partnership or a sponsor/carrier network JV with explicit customer ownership and funding responsibilities.
carriers.what_carrier_gets: Potential incremental fixed-broadband reach and a platform for converged customer acquisition, subject to exact overlap and retail conversion economics.
carriers.what_oak_hill_gets: Potential retail distribution, customer monetization and shared build capital, balanced against wholesale margin and control ceded.
carriers.challenge: Existing fiber commitments compete for capital and integration capacity. Prove incremental geography relative to all T-Mobile fiber partners. Do not infer that the same sponsor or similar asset guarantees another deal.
diligence: Address-level overlap with Metronet, Lumos, pending GoNetspeed/Greenlight and i3 perimeters
Existing retail customers versus premises and construction backlog
Minimum volume, take-or-pay, wholesale pricing and capex obligations
Assignability of MDU, municipal, grant and customer contracts

carriers.name: Verizon

public_facts.claim: Eaton agreement places funding, network build, maintenance and installation with Eaton; Verizon handles retail sales, marketing and customer service, with residential retail exclusivity through construction and an additional period.
Starry acquisition announced as an MDU strategy in five major markets; Verizon's June 2026 filing confirms Starry closed January 30, 2026 and Frontier January 20, 2026.

carriers.pitch_inference: A package outside the combined Fios/Frontier fiber footprint, with verified MDU access and a credible build operator, has a relevant commercial precedent. The precedent demonstrates a model, not Verizon interest in Omni.
carriers.best_structure_hypothesis: Market-specific, externally funded wholesale build agreement, tested against a whole-platform alternative.
carriers.what_carrier_gets: Potential new broadband markets and a delivery partner; MDU access would need to solve a demonstrable property-access or installation bottleneck.
carriers.what_oak_hill_gets: Potential anchor demand while retaining network ownership; returns depend on contract pricing, funding burden and exclusivity.
carriers.challenge: Frontier broadens overlap, and Starry provides an existing MDU capability. A fiber MDU thesis must explain its incremental value beyond these assets; shared markets alone do not demonstrate competitive whitespace.
diligence: Property rights and wiring ownership, rather than county apartment counts
Carrier economics after wholesale discount and exclusivity
Construction obligations and residual value after exclusivity expires

carriers.name: AT&T / Gigapower / commercial open access

public_facts.claim: AT&T closed the Lumen mass-markets fiber acquisition February 2, 2026, adding more than one million fiber subscribers and more than four million fiber locations. Management links fiber reach with converged wireless acquisition and retention.
AT&T has used organic builds, its Gigapower JV, commercial open-access agreements and public-private programs as distinct expansion models.

carriers.pitch_inference: Test market-level access outside AT&T's actual fiber availability rather than marketing every Omni/Lit state as incremental. A commercial access contract may be more plausible than buying an entire mixed-perimeter operator.
carriers.best_structure_hypothesis: Selected-market open-access or anchor-tenant agreement with audited available addresses and conversion economics.
carriers.what_carrier_gets: Potential incremental fiber availability at a contracted cost, with access to its existing national wireless distribution.
carriers.what_oak_hill_gets: Potential incremental network utilization and distribution, offset by wholesale discounts and any operating requirements.
carriers.challenge: AT&T already operates broadly in Ohio, Michigan and Texas, while Quantum/Lumen changes the perimeter further. Incumbent territory is not the same as exact fiber overlap, but neither is a state label evidence of whitespace.
diligence: Exact fiber overlap and announced build competition
Retail pricing, promotion and wholesale net revenue
Address eligibility, install SLA and customer transfer costs

capital.type: Analytical framework; no company valuation or financing commitment implied
capital.build_vs_buy: Compare acquisition equity plus assumed debt, integration costs and funded/unfunded completion capex with the risk-adjusted cost and time of building equivalent incremental serviceable addresses. Existing customers and cash flow must be valued separately from vacant available addresses.
capital.carrier_jv: Separate seller cash at close, retained network equity, future equity calls, customer-book value and wholesale network cash flow. A headline carrier investment is not a whole-company valuation when it also purchases customers or funds future growth.
capital.mdu_unit_economics: Annual contribution per activated unit equals twelve times net monthly revenue less unit-level recurring service and property payments; recovery period uses total incremental connection and common-area capital, not only drop cost. Corporate overhead, churn and replacement capex remain separate.
capital.acquisition_capacity: Require drawn debt, cash, availability conditions, leverage tests and committed construction funding before sizing cash M&A. The announced $1.6 billion Rightfiber facility is a relevant funding precedent, not calculated acquisition headroom.

rightfiber.title: Buy incremental reach and customer economics.
rightfiber.lede: Ritter and Great Plains now form one Grain-backed platform. The Southern screen favors coherent last-mile clusters, measurable customer value and executable ownership structures.
rightfiber.decision: Separate small contiguous bolt-ons from capital-intensive development platforms and cooperative partnerships. Size acquisition funding only after committed construction and facility headroom are known.

targets.name: NATCO Communications, Inc.
targets.owner: Independent, locally operated; NATCO says third-generation Sanders family remains involved. No public sale announcement found in this bounded pass.
clusters: Boone 2,132 and Marion 3,441 D25 FTTP availability locations; NATCO also markets parts of Baxter, but its D25 filer had no Baxter FTTP records.
targets.regionalPriority: 1: high partnership; medium, contingent M&A
publicFacts: Independent, locally operated; NATCO says third-generation Sanders family remains involved. No public sale announcement found in this bounded pass.
buildEvidence: USDA approved a $3.287 million FY2024 grant plus $0.493 million additional funding for Marion County FTTP benefiting 242 residents and two businesses.
NATCO reports $12.7 million of BEAD projects underway/planned for 1,500+ locations. Arkansas lists an E. Ritter/NATCO BEAD pre-registration partnership; scope and award status were not located.
scale: 5,573 unique FCC FTTP availability locations, not passings or subscribers (D25 2025-12-31; revised 2026-09-15)
targets.fit: Best immediate partner. It fills a north-central gap where Rightfiber reported only five Boone locations, and the BEAD partnership is a demonstrated channel. Local ownership and funded builds favor partnership before M&A.
targets.structure: Explore on transport, construction, purchasing, managed services, and grant execution. Keep minority investment or acquisition as a family-initiated option only.
targets.constraint: Ozark density/terrain; USDA/BEAD obligations; ILEC/ETC approvals; family governance; small-system economics.
targets.countercase: NATCO may gain sufficient scale through cooperation without selling, while Rightfiber is still integrating its September merger.
targets.geographyDefinition: States referenced in this research, which may include service, construction, planned markets or enterprise endpoints. Stage remains in the evidence; this is not a uniform retail footprint.

targets.name: Yelcot Holding Group, Inc. / Mountain View Telephone Company
targets.owner: Yelcot Telephone, Mountain View Telephone, and Yelcot Video remain under Yelcot Holding Group; the site says locally operated. Beneficial ownership was not verified and no transaction announcement was found.
clusters: Baxter 3,264; Stone 2,802; Marion 2,280; Independence 2,076; Izard 1,467; smaller Cleburne, Sharp, Searcy, and White records.
targets.regionalPriority: 2: high fit; medium near-term actionability
publicFacts: Yelcot Telephone, Mountain View Telephone, and Yelcot Video remain under Yelcot Holding Group; the site says locally operated. Beneficial ownership was not verified and no transaction announcement was found.
buildEvidence: USDA awarded Mountain View Telephone a $25.281 million FY2024 FTTP loan benefiting 2,630 people, 46 businesses, 124 farms, and six educational facilities in Izard and Stone. FCC shows 7,323 tentative E-ACAM required locations through 2028.
scale: 12,274 unique FCC FTTP availability locations, not passings or subscribers (D25 2025-12-31; revised 2026-09-15)
targets.fit: Best scaled footprint. It extends Rightfiber through the Ozarks and overlaps its Independence presence. Marion overlap with NATCO requires address-level analysis.
targets.structure: Start with interconnection, backhaul, enterprise referrals, field support, or grant construction; consider holdco acquisition after ownership and subsidy diligence.

buildEvidence: Dragonfly completed its acquisition of Myakka Communications on December 24, 2025, adding rural eastern Manatee and Sarasota counties in western Florida. Dragonfly's March 2026 Fast Wireless acquisition added a fixed-wireless provider serving Monroeville, Mexia, and Frisco City, Alabama. The same release says Dragonfly covered more than 20,000 homes. That is a company-described coverage metric, not subscribers, fiber passings, or connected locations. A 2018 Florida PSC filing reported that Myakka then served more than 2,600 data customers and operated more than 500 miles of buried fiber, but those figures are stale and pre-acquisition.

Alabama’s provisional-award table in the final proposal lists SPBroadband fiber projects with3,136 Conecuh,1,369 Escambia and3,379 Monroe BSLs, totaling7,884. This is a derived scheduled BEAD amount, not proof of an executed grant, disbursed cash or total project cost. The table is PDFpage7; grant agreement, matching funds and completion remain to verify.

Dragonfly combines owned retail operations, fixed wireless and fiber, managed Wi-Fi, voice, and an open-access policy for its fiber network. Its network policy says the entire fiber network is available to outside carriers, including portions not built with federal grants. The record does not show signed wholesale tenants or wholesale revenue.

targets.name: Ubiquity / FiberFirst
targets.owner: Ubiquity owns and develops multi-tenant open-access infrastructure and describes FiberFirst as its owned retail ISP; Generate Capital and 1248 Holdings are disclosed equity sponsors
clusters: Omaha NE; Dallas–Fort Worth / Austin TX; exact infrastructure versus retail perimeter needs confirmation
publicFacts: Ubiquity owns and develops multi-tenant open-access infrastructure and describes FiberFirst as its owned retail ISP; Generate Capital and 1248 Holdings are disclosed equity sponsors

The wholesale and retail layers are distinct in function but linked by ownership. Ubiquity builds multi-tenant open-access fiber and supports lit and dark-fiber tenants. FiberFirst sells residential and business internet over Ubiquity networks and serves as Ubiquity's speed-to-market retail tenant. Treating FiberFirst as merely an unaffiliated customer would be incorrect.
buildEvidence: FiberFirst currently lists service across Arizona, California, Nebraska, and Texas. Nebraska retail launched in Omaha in November 2023 after an October soft launch, initially naming Dundee, Benson, Morton Meadows, and Florence. In Texas, FiberFirst lists DFW and central-Texas communities including Fort Worth, Keller, Southlake, Georgetown, Hutto, Killeen, Liberty Hill, and Taylor.

Texas build evidence includes a planned $75 million Georgetown citywide network announced in December 2021 and a further $100 million for Hutto and Killeen announced in February 2022. These are announced investment plans, not audited capital deployed. Ubiquity's Nebraska tariff, effective November 14, 2022, separately documents dark-fiber interconnect, transport, and backhaul services.

Ubiquity reported $420 million of construction financing in December 2024, consisting of a $275 million construction facility and a $145 million revolving facility. In May 2025, it upsized the construction facility to $350 million, an incremental $75 million. These are facilities, not amounts drawn or invested, and the May release does not restate the revolver's contemporaneous balance or availability.

Ubiquity said in December 2024 that it had delivered hundreds of thousands of addresses across Texas, California, Arizona, and Nebraska. The wording does not define whether delivered addresses means constructed passings, marketable locations, or addresses released to tenants, and it discloses no subscribers or FiberFirst penetration.

AT&T announced wholesale access to Ubiquity's multi-state network, targeted builds for MDUs and HOAs, and exclusive greenfield areas initially in Minnesota. That validates a second-tenant and national private-access model, but public sources do not disclose economics, exact committed locations, minimum volumes, or how exclusivity applies by market.
scale: Hundreds of thousands of addresses delivered across Texas, California, Arizona and Nebraska, company-reported 2024-12-17; 'delivered' is undefined and is not treated as subscribers or a comparable passing count.
$420 million of construction financing announced 2024-12-17, comprising a $275 million construction facility and a $145 million revolving facility; facility capacity, not drawn debt or capital spent.
$350 million construction facility after a $75 million upsize announced 2025-05-13; the release does not update the contemporaneous balance or availability of the separate revolver.
$75 million Georgetown plan announced 2021-12-15 and an additional $100 million Hutto/Killeen plan announced 2022-02-02; announced investment plans, not audited deployed capital.
targets.fit: Strongest direct geographic adjacency in Omaha and Texas, plus a differentiated wholesale/open-access model and existing multi-tenant carrier framework
targets.structure: Selected infrastructure or retail perimeter, wholesale access, or sponsor-level combination; reconcile the AT&T anchor and retail channel before structuring.
targets.constraint: Retail overlap, an AT&T wholesale agreement, sponsor-backed financing, and unclear legal or economic separability between infrastructure and FiberFirst raise perimeter and conflict complexity
targets.countercase: Countercase: Omaha and Texas also create retail overlap, FiberFirst is an owned ISP rather than a clean independent tenant, and Ubiquity has large sponsor-backed financing plus a material AT&T relationship. Public sources do not establish that the infrastructure, FiberFirst customers, state entities, financing, or carrier contracts can be separated. Any strategic perimeter would require asset, tenant, exclusivity, debt, and change-of-control diligence.

scale: Public fact: at 2025-12-31 Uniti reported approximately 240,000 fiber route miles, 11.2 million fiber strand miles, 282,000 copper route miles, more than 1.0 million customers, more than 500,000 residential fiber customers, and approximately 1.9 million fiber-equipped households. Operating lease liabilities were $483.1 million at 2025-12-31, but that balance is not a fiber-mile measure. Uniti sells or grants dark fiber through leases and IRUs and also operates owned builds. A data-center count is not disclosed; the 10-K instead describes on-net colocation facilities and key data-center corridors. targets.fit: Analytical inference: Uniti is the most capable national wholesale counterpart and the least credible conventional bolt-on. A combined RightFiber/Great Plains platform could explore reciprocal transport, wavelength, dark-fiber, colocation, or customer-backed joint builds where actual endpoints justify them. Uniti's Tier 2 and Tier 3 strategy and Midwest/Southeast access may be commercially adjacent, but no route overlap or customer synergy is established here. The post-merger company reported no single customer or related group at 10% or more of 2025 consolidated revenue, which reduces the old Windstream concentration issue at the consolidated level, but segment-level and contract-level concentration remain undisclosed. [S2]
targets.structure: Priority route: wholesale or customer-backed joint build first. Second route: a narrow asset carveout only if Uniti identifies non-core assets and title, debt collateral, easements, operating systems, customers, and transition services can be separated. Management said on 2026-07-30 that it may monetize non-core assets, but did not identify a process or perimeter. Full acquisition would require public-company control, refinancing or assumption of a highly levered capital structure, and integration of consumer, managed-services, copper, wholesale, and enterprise operations. It is a transformational transaction far beyond a normal regional add-on. [S3]
targets.constraint: Public fact: Q2 2026 net loss was $155.9 million, notes and other debt were $10.65 billion net at 2026-06-30, and 2026 interest-expense guidance was $805 million. Uniti is simultaneously funding Kinetic fiber construction and Fiber Infrastructure expansion and had used nearly $3 billion of asset securitizations by July 2026. After quarter-end, the issuers accepted $480.236 million aggregate principal amount of secured notes for purchase under asset sale offers on 2026-08-21; this is a debt-reduction event, not evidence that a new operating-asset sale process is open. Indebtedness can constrain flexibility, while securitization, debt repayment, and possible asset monetization expand financing options. Any carveout must clear debt documents and ABS collateral boundaries. Customer, ROW, pole, IRU, lease, and regulatory transferability are unknown until diligence. [S3, S16]
targets.countercase: Countercase: scale is also the strategic argument. Uniti owns, operates, or leases a nationwide network, offers 10 to 400 Gbps waves, spectrum, dark fiber, Ethernet, internet, colocation, enterprise managed networking, and wireless backhaul, and has no disclosed consolidated customer above 10% of revenue after the merger. If a buyer wanted a national platform rather than a regional adjacency, Uniti would be uniquely broad. That thesis still has to overcome leverage, public-company execution, integration risk, copper and legacy-service exposure, and the absence of a verified sale process. [S2, S3]

A partnership could provide Northeast reach and Canadian gateways without acquiring a large, noncontiguous operating company. More than 15,000 businesses reportedly rely on FirstLight, but private-company revenue, EBITDA, top-customer concentration, churn, and contract tenure are not disclosed. The named hyperscaler award proves capability, not diversification or concentration. [S5, S7]
targets.structure: Priority route: wholesale interconnection, resale, protected wave, or route-specific dark-fiber cooperation tied to customer demand. Full acquisition is conceivable only as a sponsor-led exit from Antin Fund III, but holding vintage is not evidence of availability. It would be a large platform acquisition with six-state operations, data centers, cloud, voice, unified communications, security, and managed services, not an easy bolt-on. Asset carveout is less natural because FirstLight describes an integrated owned and operated network. A route or data-center carveout would require proof that customers, transport, regeneration sites, systems, employees, and permits can be separated without damaging the remaining network. It also described rapid expansion across five core U.S. markets. The network is purpose-built for data-center, hyperscaler, cloud, carrier, large-enterprise, and government connectivity. [S10] The current site calls the more than 1,200-mile network newly built, high-count, 100% underground, fully owned, operated, and maintained by SummitIG. scale: Public fact: current company materials state more than 1,200 operational route miles, 100% underground. The 2026-06-30 transaction release instead says the pre-acquisition Virginia footprint exceeded 1,100 miles and DF&I added nearly 200 miles of conduit and dark-fiber assets. These figures should not be added mechanically because geography, operating status, and overlap are not reconciled. [S10, S11] The disclosed product is predominantly dark fiber and custom infrastructure rather than a broad lit enterprise suite. No revenue, EBITDA, capex, debt, customer count, fiber-pair inventory, route utilization, or data-center count is publicly disclosed. targets.fit: Analytical inference: SummitIG is the strongest specialist route to data-center and hyperscale ecosystems, but the weakest conventional enterprise bolt-on. Columbus and Chicago could be commercially relevant to a broader Midwestern strategy, yet no location overlap with Great Plains or RightFiber is established. A customer-backed dark-fiber, metro cross-connect, or joint-build relationship could let the combined platform connect enterprise customers into SummitIG's data-center routes while preserving each operator's core. SummitIG's custom hyperscale focus creates possible customer-concentration risk, but neither concentration nor contract economics are public. That risk must be labeled unknown, not assumed high. [S10, S11]
targets.structure: Priority route: route-specific wholesale, IRU, lateral, or joint-build cooperation where named customer endpoints create demand. Full acquisition would require negotiating with a majority sponsor and potentially multiple minority holders, funding a scaled data-center fiber platform, and absorbing active construction and DF&I integration. It is not an easy bolt-on. Asset carveout is strategically counter to SummitIG's current density and corridor-integration program unless an owner affirmatively offers a non-core geography. The SierraIG precedent proves SummitIG will use a JV structure, but it does not imply willingness to form a U.S. JV with these buyers. No public sale process was found. [S10, S13, S15]
targets.constraint: Unknown: private-company debt, cash, leverage, EBITDA, maintenance capex, committed build capital, and customer concentration. Public evidence points to capital access, not unlimited capacity: SDC reported approximately $12 billion of AUM in the June 2026 release, the platform has institutional minority backing, and it completed DF&I while funding multi-market expansion. Constraints include integrating acquired records and customers, finishing committed construction, permit and ROW execution, serving high-count custom contracts, and avoiding stranded speculative routes. Minority-holder rights and SDC's 'Partially Realized' designation require direct diligence. [S10, S14]
targets.countercase: Countercase: SummitIG's owner-operator model, underground high-count infrastructure, Northern Virginia density, Columbus build, Chicago expansion, and DF&I corridor can be more valuable as a specialist partner or standalone platform than as part of a regional enterprise operator. Recent acquisition activity and active expansion are evidence of a growth posture, not a divestiture posture. Conversely, SDC's partial realization history means a future ownership event is plausible in principle. Neither point establishes current availability, valuation, or process. [S10, S11, S14]

The wholesale and retail layers are distinct in function but linked by ownership. Ubiquity builds multi-tenant open-access fiber and supports lit and dark-fiber tenants. FiberFirst sells residential and business internet over Ubiquity networks and serves as Ubiquity's speed-to-market retail tenant. Treating FiberFirst as merely an unaffiliated customer would be incorrect.
buildEvidence: FiberFirst currently lists service across Arizona, California, Nebraska, and Texas. Nebraska retail launched in Omaha in November 2023 after an October soft launch, initially naming Dundee, Benson, Morton Meadows, and Florence. In Texas, FiberFirst lists DFW and central-Texas communities including Fort Worth, Keller, Southlake, Georgetown, Hutto, Killeen, Liberty Hill, and Taylor.

Texas build evidence includes a planned $75 million Georgetown citywide network announced in December 2021 and a further $100 million for Hutto and Killeen announced in February 2022. These are announced investment plans, not audited capital deployed. Ubiquity's Nebraska tariff, effective November 14, 2022, separately documents dark-fiber interconnect, transport, and backhaul services.

Ubiquity reported $420 million of construction financing in December 2024, consisting of a $275 million construction facility and a $145 million revolving facility. In May 2025, it upsized the construction facility to $350 million, an incremental $75 million. These are facilities, not amounts drawn or invested, and the May release does not restate the revolver's contemporaneous balance or availability.

Ubiquity said in December 2024 that it had delivered hundreds of thousands of addresses across Texas, California, Arizona, and Nebraska. The wording does not define whether delivered addresses means constructed passings, marketable locations, or addresses released to tenants, and it discloses no subscribers or FiberFirst penetration.

AT&T announced wholesale access to Ubiquity's multi-state network, targeted builds for MDUs and HOAs, and exclusive greenfield areas initially in Minnesota. That validates a second-tenant and national private-access model, but public sources do not disclose economics, exact committed locations, minimum volumes, or how exclusivity applies by market.

acceleratedAnalyses.title: Midwest ownership, build stages and transaction watch
acceleratedAnalyses.summary: Prioritize owner-verified commercial routes with Joink, Metro, Midwest Fiber Networks, WIN Technology and selected Iowa, Missouri and Kentucky operators. Keep recent consolidators, cooperatives and public-company platforms in separate lanes, and do not count announced acquisitions as closed. The Illinois/Indiana reconciliation separates acquired names from measured FCC filers and shows where row counts and corporate rollups can inflate the apparent footprint.
acceleratedAnalyses.scope: Public-source review as of September 20, 2026. The operator screen covers Illinois and Indiana plus selected Wisconsin, Iowa, Missouri, Kentucky, Michigan, Ohio and Kansas platform cases. County names identify public footprint or project clusters, not route connections, physical diversity, enterprise availability or seller willingness. Scale is stated only with its source date and unit. A bounded IL/IN appendix independently audits 16 legal-filer/state rows across 11 operator cases and four exact selected-set location unions using retained D25 inputs. targets.name: Uniti Group Inc. (post-Windstream perimeter)
targets.owner: Public fact: the merger closed on 2025-08-01. Legacy Uniti and Windstream became indirect wholly owned subsidiaries of the listed parent, Uniti Group Inc. Legacy Uniti holders received approximately 62% of the combined common stock at closing and legacy Windstream holders approximately 38%, before convertible securities and warrants. Uniti trades on Nasdaq as UNIT. This is a public-company control situation, not a sponsor exit. [S1, S2]
clusters: National wholesale backbone and optical transport, Kinetic local access concentrated in the Midwest and Southeast, and enterprise fiber markets across the Southeast. [S2]

Current named growth nodes include Jackson, Birmingham, Huntsville, Montgomery, Tulsa, and South-Central long-haul routes. In 2026 Uniti disclosed a 69-route-mile Birmingham metro build, a Tulsa 50-rack colocation agreement, and a broader 1,100-route-mile South-Central expansion or upgrade program. The 1,100 miles are an announced program, not all confirmed completed miles. [S4]
targets.regionalPriority: High for a bounded wholesale or joint-build discussion after route-level validation; medium-low for a specifically offered non-core carveout; low for full acquisition under the stated regional-platform objective.
publicFacts: Public fact: the merger closed on 2025-08-01. Legacy Uniti and Windstream became indirect wholly owned subsidiaries of the listed parent, Uniti Group Inc. Legacy Uniti holders received approximately 62% of the combined common stock at closing and legacy Windstream holders approximately 38%, before convertible securities and warrants. Uniti trades on Nasdaq as UNIT. This is a public-company control situation, not a sponsor exit. [S1, S2]
buildEvidence: Public fact: Uniti is executing customer-aligned high-count long-haul, metro-lateral, dark-fiber, optical-wave, and colocation expansion. At 2026 Q2, Fiber Infrastructure recorded about $2.2 million of new monthly recurring revenue bookings, its reported record, and $77.2 million of quarterly capital expenditure before $9.7 million of customer upfront payments. The company also disclosed a 20-year, $500 million customer contract in May 2026, without naming the customer. These facts show active build and contracting, not asset availability. [S3, S4]
scale: Public fact: at 2025-12-31 Uniti reported approximately 240,000 fiber route miles, 11.2 million fiber strand miles, 282,000 copper route miles, more than 1.0 million customers, more than 500,000 residential fiber customers, and approximately 1.9 million fiber-equipped households. The property disclosure says the group 'own[s] or lease[s]' the fiber miles and does not publish an owned-versus-leased route-mile split. Operating lease liabilities were $483.1 million at 2025-12-31, but that balance is not a fiber-mile measure. Uniti sells or grants dark fiber through leases and IRUs and also operates owned builds. A data-center count is not disclosed; the 10-K instead describes on-net colocation facilities and key data-center corridors. [S2] At 2026-06-30 the company reported $12.98 billion of assets, $608.9 million of cash, and $10.65 billion of notes and other debt, net. [S3]
targets.fit: Analytical inference: Uniti is the most capable national wholesale counterpart and the least credible conventional bolt-on. A combined RightFiber/Great Plains platform could explore reciprocal transport, wavelength, dark-fiber, colocation, or customer-backed joint builds where actual endpoints justify them. Uniti's Tier 2 and Tier 3 strategy and Midwest/Southeast access may be commercially adjacent, but no route overlap or customer synergy is established here. The post-merger company reported no single customer or related group at 10% or more of 2025 consolidated revenue, which reduces the old Windstream concentration issue at the consolidated level, but segment-level and contract-level concentration remain undisclosed. [S2]
targets.structure: Priority route: wholesale or customer-backed joint build first. Second route: a narrow asset carveout only if Uniti identifies non-core assets and title, debt collateral, easements, operating systems, customers, and transition services can be separated. Management said on 2026-07-30 that it may monetize non-core assets, but did not identify a process or perimeter. Full acquisition would require public-company control, refinancing or assumption of a highly levered capital structure, and integration of consumer, managed-services, copper, wholesale, and enterprise operations. It is a transformational transaction far beyond a normal regional add-on. [S3]
targets.constraint: Public fact: Q2 2026 net loss was $155.9 million, notes and other debt were $10.65 billion net at 2026-06-30, and 2026 interest-expense guidance was $805 million. Uniti is simultaneously funding Kinetic fiber construction and Fiber Infrastructure expansion and had used nearly $3 billion of asset securitizations by July 2026. After quarter-end, the issuers accepted $480.236 million aggregate principal amount of secured notes for purchase under asset sale offers on 2026-08-21; this is a debt-reduction event, not evidence that a new operating-asset sale process is open. Indebtedness can constrain flexibility, while securitization, debt repayment, and possible asset monetization expand financing options. Any carveout must clear debt documents and ABS collateral boundaries. Customer, ROW, pole, IRU, lease, and regulatory transferability are unknown until diligence. [S3, S16]
targets.countercase: Countercase: scale is also the strategic argument. Uniti owns, operates, or leases a nationwide network, offers 10 to 400 Gbps waves, spectrum, dark fiber, Ethernet, internet, colocation, enterprise managed networking, and wireless backhaul, and has no disclosed consolidated customer above 10% of revenue after the merger. If a buyer wanted a national platform rather than a regional adjacency, Uniti would be uniquely broad. That thesis still has to overcome leverage, public-company execution, integration risk, copper and legacy-service exposure, and the absence of a verified sale process. [S2, S3]
geographicScopeNotes: Public fact: approximately 240,000 fiber route miles across 47 U.S. states at 2025-12-31. The 10-K describes fiber-equipped households predominantly in the Midwest and Southeast. [S2]
Public fact: 2026 expansion evidence includes Mississippi, Alabama, and Oklahoma. [S4]
Unknown: this screen did not perform a location-level overlay against RightFiber or Great Plains. State presence is not evidence of route or building overlap.

targets.name: FirstLight Fiber / Antin Infrastructure Partners
targets.owner: Public fact: Antin agreed to acquire FirstLight from Oak Hill on 2018-02-21, with closing then expected in the second half of 2018. Antin's 2025 Universal Registration Document still lists FirstLight in Flagship Fund III and III-B, investment year 2018, confirming the current fund perimeter at 2025-12-31. FirstLight is private. No reviewed primary source announced a current sale process. [S8, S9]
clusters: Dense Northeast and northern Mid-Atlantic corridors, including Albany-Boston, New York State, northern New England, Pennsylvania, and Canadian connectivity. Albany is described as a regeneration and colocation point on the 240-route-mile Albany-Boston hyperscaler route announced 2026-09-17. [S5]

The current data-center page names five featured locations and nine additional location names, with Manchester appearing in both lists. It therefore supports 13 unique named locations, not a clean 14-facility count, and does not disclose ownership versus leased colocation at every site. [S7]
targets.regionalPriority: Medium-high for wholesale extension if customers need Northeast or Canadian reach; medium only as a full-platform sponsor event if Antin chooses to transact; low for an unsolicited carveout absent separability evidence.
publicFacts: Public fact: Antin agreed to acquire FirstLight from Oak Hill on 2018-02-21, with closing then expected in the second half of 2018. Antin's 2025 Universal Registration Document still lists FirstLight in Flagship Fund III and III-B, investment year 2018, confirming the current fund perimeter at 2025-12-31. FirstLight is private. No reviewed primary source announced a current sale process. [S8, S9]
buildEvidence: Public fact: FirstLight announced a major hyperscaler agreement on 2026-09-17 for a 240-route-mile high-fiber-count Albany-Boston route. The company completed a Brunswick, Maine data-center expansion in February 2025 and selected a new network system of record in August 2026. These are operating and modernization signals. They do not establish that FirstLight is for sale or that a particular route is separable. [S5, S7]
scale: Material conflict: the newest dated company release says 20,000 route miles across six states and the current site footer says the same, connecting more than 16,000 on-net locations. A 2025 company white paper and multiple current data-center cards instead say approximately 25,000 route miles; the white paper adds nearly 15,000 lit locations and access to another 125,000 and calls the network exclusively owned and operated. [S5, S6, S7] Use 20,000 as the latest dated stated perimeter, but do not treat the discrepancy as resolved. The 'exclusively owned and operated' claim is marketing-level evidence, not a route-by-route title schedule, and no leased fiber, IRU, pole, conduit, or facility mix is published. Featured data-center sizes range from 3,260 square feet at Rockland to 52,000 square feet at Brunswick; a total facility-area figure is not disclosed. [S7]
targets.fit: Analytical inference: FirstLight could add a coherent Northeast enterprise, carrier, dark-fiber, cloud, managed-services, and colocation region. For a combined RightFiber/Great Plains platform, that is a geographic extension rather than a proven infill. A partnership could provide Northeast reach and Canadian gateways without acquiring a large, noncontiguous operating company. More than 15,000 businesses reportedly rely on FirstLight, but private-company revenue, EBITDA, top-customer concentration, churn, and contract tenure are not disclosed. The named hyperscaler award proves capability, not diversification or concentration. [S5, S7]
targets.structure: Priority route: wholesale interconnection, resale, protected wave, or route-specific dark-fiber cooperation tied to customer demand. Full acquisition is conceivable only as a sponsor-led exit from Antin Fund III, but holding vintage is not evidence of availability. It would be a large platform acquisition with six-state operations, data centers, cloud, voice, unified communications, security, and managed services, not an easy bolt-on. Asset carveout is less natural because FirstLight describes an integrated owned and operated network. A route or data-center carveout would require proof that customers, transport, regeneration sites, systems, employees, and permits can be separated without damaging the remaining network. No such public offer was found. [S5, S8, S9]
targets.constraint: Unknown: FirstLight does not publish debt, liquidity, capex, EBITDA, leverage, or fund-level asset valuation. Antin's funds are closed-ended and FirstLight has been held since 2018, which creates eventual monetization logic as a general fund-life inference, but no exit timetable or process is public. The current 20,000-versus-25,000 route-mile conflict is a diligence issue. Other diligence priorities are owned-versus-IRU routes, data-center title and power commitments, customer concentration, carrier and hyperscaler contract terms, pension and labor exposure, network rationalization, and the capital required for high-count route upgrades.
targets.countercase: Countercase: the platform is operationally coherent, already sells the full enterprise and wholesale stack, has a dense six-state route system, more than 16,000 stated on-net locations, and a tangible data-center estate. Those attributes could justify full-platform value for a buyer deliberately pursuing a multi-region strategy. The contrary evidence is geographic separation, unreported leverage and earnings, inconsistent public scale data, a mature sponsor owner that may require a full value realization, and no public indication that a whole-company or asset sale is available. [S5, S7, S8]
geographicScopeNotes: Public fact: the latest dated company release, 2026-09-17, defines the core six-state network as Maine, New Hampshire, Vermont, New York, Massachusetts, and Pennsylvania. [S5]
Public fact: FirstLight also markets routes to Secaucus, Toronto, and Montreal, but those connections should not be converted into owned-state footprint without an asset map and title schedule.
Unknown: no building- or route-level overlap with RightFiber or Great Plains was tested in this screen.

targets.name: SummitIG
targets.owner: Public fact: SDC Capital Partners has been SummitIG's majority owner since 2019, reaffirmed in the 2026 DF&I acquisition release. In 2021 Harrison Street acquired a significant minority interest and Columbia Capital retained a minority interest. The latest primary release does not restate those minority positions, so their current percentages and continuing status are unknown. SDC's current portfolio page labels SummitIG 'Partially Realized' while still listing it as an investment. That label is consistent with prior partial monetization but is not a current sale-process announcement. [S10, S13, S14]
clusters: Northern Virginia is the anchor and densest cluster. SummitIG reported more than 1,100 miles of Virginia infrastructure before integrating nearly 200 miles of DF&I conduit and dark fiber, including nearly 60 miles of distinct Maryland reach to Baltimore, on 2026-06-30. [S10]

The current company site reports more than 1,200 operational miles across Northern Virginia, Greater Virginia, Columbus, Chicago, and other new markets. It separately states more than 200 newly constructed miles in Columbus, more than 175 long-haul miles from Northern Virginia toward Richmond, and more than 60 Chicago miles with 100 miles under development. The site does not provide a reliable numeric data-center or on-net-building count in accessible static text. [S11, S12]
targets.regionalPriority: High for customer-led data-center dark-fiber cooperation after route validation; low-medium for full acquisition if a sponsor-led process actually emerges; low for an unsolicited asset carveout.
publicFacts: Public fact: SDC Capital Partners has been SummitIG's majority owner since 2019, reaffirmed in the 2026 DF&I acquisition release. In 2021 Harrison Street acquired a significant minority interest and Columbia Capital retained a minority interest. The latest primary release does not restate those minority positions, so their current percentages and continuing status are unknown. SDC's current portfolio page labels SummitIG 'Partially Realized' while still listing it as an investment. That label is consistent with prior partial monetization but is not a current sale-process announcement. [S10, S13, S14]
buildEvidence: Public fact: SummitIG completed the acquisition of DF&I from Blue Owl-managed funds on 2026-06-30 and said it was integrating customers, operations, network records, and remaining active construction. It also described rapid expansion across five core U.S. markets. The network is purpose-built for data-center, hyperscaler, cloud, carrier, large-enterprise, and government connectivity. [S10] The current site calls the more than 1,200-mile network newly built, high-count, 100% underground, fully owned, operated, and maintained by SummitIG. [S11] Those claims support control of the physical network but do not disclose conduit leases, ROW terms, laterals, or customer IRUs.
scale: Public fact: current company materials state more than 1,200 operational route miles, 100% underground. The 2026-06-30 transaction release instead says the pre-acquisition Virginia footprint exceeded 1,100 miles and DF&I added nearly 200 miles of conduit and dark-fiber assets. These figures should not be added mechanically because geography, operating status, and overlap are not reconciled. [S10, S11] The disclosed product is predominantly dark fiber and custom infrastructure rather than a broad lit enterprise suite. No revenue, EBITDA, capex, debt, customer count, fiber-pair inventory, route utilization, or data-center count is publicly disclosed. SierraIG's 750 km target and $50 million investment target remain announced plans from 2024. [S15]
targets.fit: Analytical inference: SummitIG is the strongest specialist route to data-center and hyperscale ecosystems, but the weakest conventional enterprise bolt-on. Columbus and Chicago could be commercially relevant to a broader Midwestern strategy, yet no location overlap with Great Plains or RightFiber is established. A customer-backed dark-fiber, metro cross-connect, or joint-build relationship could let the combined platform connect enterprise customers into SummitIG's data-center routes while preserving each operator's core. SummitIG's custom hyperscale focus creates possible customer-concentration risk, but neither concentration nor contract economics are public. That risk must be labeled unknown, not assumed high. [S10, S11]
targets.structure: Priority route: route-specific wholesale, IRU, lateral, or joint-build cooperation where named customer endpoints create demand. Full acquisition would require negotiating with a majority sponsor and potentially multiple minority holders, funding a scaled data-center fiber platform, and absorbing active construction and DF&I integration. It is not an easy bolt-on. Asset carveout is strategically counter to SummitIG's current density and corridor-integration program unless an owner affirmatively offers a non-core geography. The SierraIG precedent proves SummitIG will use a JV structure, but it does not imply willingness to form a U.S. JV with these buyers. No public sale process was found. [S10, S13, S15]
targets.constraint: Unknown: private-company debt, cash, leverage, EBITDA, maintenance capex, committed build capital, and customer concentration. Public evidence points to capital access, not unlimited capacity: SDC reported approximately $12 billion of AUM in the June 2026 release, the platform has institutional minority backing, and it completed DF&I while funding multi-market expansion. Constraints include integrating acquired records and customers, finishing committed construction, permit and ROW execution, serving high-count custom contracts, and avoiding stranded speculative routes. Minority-holder rights and SDC's 'Partially Realized' designation require direct diligence. [S10, S14]
targets.countercase: Countercase: SummitIG's owner-operator model, underground high-count infrastructure, Northern Virginia density, Columbus build, Chicago expansion, and DF&I corridor can be more valuable as a specialist partner or standalone platform than as part of a regional enterprise operator. Recent acquisition activity and active expansion are evidence of a growth posture, not a divestiture posture. Conversely, SDC's partial realization history means a future ownership event is plausible in principle. Neither point establishes current availability, valuation, or process. [S10, S11, S14]
geographicScopeNotes: Public fact, operational or acquired: Virginia, Maryland, Ohio, and Illinois. Core corridors are Northern Virginia, broader Virginia to Richmond, Columbus, Chicago, and the acquired Northern Virginia-to-Baltimore DF&I corridor. [S10, S11, S12]

Public fact, announced or status-uncertain: Salt Lake City, Utah and Phoenix, Arizona appear as expansion markets, but the network page also labels them coming soon. They are not treated here as fully operational mileage. [S12]

Separate perimeter: SierraIG is a majority-owned joint venture with Neutral Networks in Mexico, targeting Queretaro and Monterrey. Its 750 km and $50 million figures were 2024 plans, not actual completed scale. [S15]

Dragonfly's March 2026 Fast Wireless acquisition added a fixed-wireless provider serving Monroeville, Mexia, and Frisco City, Alabama. The same release says Dragonfly covered more than 20,000 homes. That is a company-described coverage metric, not subscribers, fiber passings, or connected locations. A 2018 Florida PSC filing reported that Myakka then served more than 2,600 data customers and operated more than 500 miles of buried fiber, but those figures are stale and pre-acquisition.

Alabama’s provisional-award table in the final proposal lists SPBroadband fiber projects with3,136 Conecuh,1,369 Escambia and3,379 Monroe BSLs, totaling7,884. Dragonfly combines owned retail operations, fixed wireless and fiber, managed Wi-Fi, voice, and an open-access policy for its fiber network. Its network policy says the entire fiber network is available to outside carriers, including portions not built with federal grants. The wholesale and retail layers are distinct in function but linked by ownership. Ubiquity builds multi-tenant open-access fiber and supports lit and dark-fiber tenants. FiberFirst sells residential and business internet over Ubiquity networks and serves as Ubiquity's speed-to-market retail tenant. Treating FiberFirst as merely an unaffiliated customer would be incorrect.
buildEvidence: FiberFirst currently lists service across Arizona, California, Nebraska, and Texas. Nebraska retail launched in Omaha in November 2023 after an October soft launch, initially naming Dundee, Benson, Morton Meadows, and Florence. In Texas, FiberFirst lists DFW and central-Texas communities including Fort Worth, Keller, Southlake, Georgetown, Hutto, Killeen, Liberty Hill, and Taylor.

Texas build evidence includes a planned $75 million Georgetown citywide network announced in December 2021 and a further $100 million for Hutto and Killeen announced in February 2022. These are announced investment plans, not audited capital deployed. Ubiquity's Nebraska tariff, effective November 14, 2022, separately documents dark-fiber interconnect, transport, and backhaul services.

Ubiquity reported $420 million of construction financing in December 2024, consisting of a $275 million construction facility and a $145 million revolving facility. In May 2025, it upsized the construction facility to $350 million, an incremental $75 million. These are facilities, not amounts drawn or invested, and the May release does not restate the revolver's contemporaneous balance or availability.

Ubiquity said in December 2024 that it had delivered hundreds of thousands of addresses across Texas, California, Arizona, and Nebraska. The wording does not define whether delivered addresses means constructed passings, marketable locations, or addresses released to tenants, and it discloses no subscribers or FiberFirst penetration.

AT&T announced wholesale access to Ubiquity's multi-state network, targeted builds for MDUs and HOAs, and exclusive greenfield areas initially in Minnesota. That validates a second-tenant and national private-access model, but public sources do not disclose economics, exact committed locations, minimum volumes, or how exclusivity applies by market.
scale: Hundreds of thousands of addresses delivered across Texas, California, Arizona and Nebraska, company-reported 2024-12-17; 'delivered' is undefined and is not treated as subscribers or a comparable passing count.
$420 million of construction financing announced 2024-12-17, comprising a $275 million construction facility and a $145 million revolving facility; facility capacity, not drawn debt or capital spent.
$350 million construction facility after a $75 million upsize announced 2025-05-13; the release does not update the contemporaneous balance or availability of the separate revolver.
$75 million Georgetown plan announced 2021-12-15 and an additional $100 million Hutto/Killeen plan announced 2022-02-02; announced investment plans, not audited deployed capital.

findings: decision: Lead with Bluebird and Sho-Me as corridor and wholesale conversations, not conventional bolt-ons. Bluebird now reports more than 36,000 route miles after buying Everstream, while Sho-Me is a cooperative-owned statewide transport mesh. Socket/Fastwyre is the cleanest Missouri FTTH adjacency, but Oak Hill and Pamlico are actively building it as a consolidator. Kingdom is the most plausible small-network partnership, but its cooperative and grant-funded perimeter makes an ordinary sale unlikely.; platform baseline: Rightfiber closed the Ritter and Great Plains combination on 2026-09-02. It reported more than 300,000 FTTH passings, a 28,000-mile fiber network whose route-versus-strand basis is not defined, more than 400 communities in 20 states, and a new $1.6 billion credit facility for organic growth and M&A. Great Plains separately markets a carrier network with more than 20,000 miles, 17,000 lit buildings, and Missouri POPs in Kansas City and St. Louis. These are company-reported figures, not independently reconciled location counts. [S01,S02]; status resolution: Bluebird completed its purchase of substantially all Everstream assets on 2026-03-06. The resulting Bluebird Fiber reports more than 36,000 route miles, more than 400,000 on-net or near-net buildings, and more than 450 POPs across 12 states. Macquarie remains the disclosed sponsor. [S03,S05]; Socket, Oak Hill and Pamlico closed the acquisition of Fastwyre's Missouri network business on 2026-04-30, per transaction adviser Houlihan Lokey. Missouri PSC records then recognized Fastwyre-to-Socket name changes in June 2026. Socket's current service list includes the acquired markets. The still-live Fastwyre customer page saying closing was pending is stale counterevidence, not the best status evidence. [S07,S08,S09,S24]; T-Mobile and Wren House announced a definitive 50/50 JV to acquire i3 on 2026-04-28. T-Mobile's 2026-07-23 Form 10-Q continued to describe the transaction as expected to close in the second half of 2026. No later primary closing announcement was found through 2026-09-20, so the transaction remains pending for this screen. [S10,S25]; Gateway Fiber's 2025 combination with WANRack and KWIKOM was operating as a unified platform by 2025-07-29. A CBRE Investment Management fund is the disclosed majority owner. [S17,S18]; Wisper's latest located ownership disclosure, in the FCC's 2024 Aristotle order, was Nathan Stooke 60% and E8 Topco 40%, with E8 supported by Digital Alpha funds. [S12]; Kingdom Telephone and Phynx Fiber consolidated branding as Kingdom Networks in 2025, but the same cooperative board and team remained. This was a name consolidation, not an acquisition. [S16]; route and product logic: [Inference] Bluebird supplies the most consequential non-GPC corridor option. Its Missouri middle-mile award describes Jefferson City-Washington, Washington-Rolla, Rolla-Strafford, and Springfield-Carthage segments, which complement GPC's Kansas City-St. Louis axis and Rightfiber's Poplar Bluff FTTH entry. Bluebird also offers dark fiber, wavelengths, carrier and hyperscale products. [S02,S03,S04,S21]; [Inference] Sho-Me is the best immediately actionable diversity partner. Its electric-transmission-line network covers more than 4,700 fiber miles and more than 120 POPs, uses ring topology, reaches rural Missouri cities, and explicitly offers carrier interconnection, wavelengths and dark fiber in some areas. [S19,S20]; [Fact] Socket, i3, Kingdom and Gateway are principally FTTH or FTTX platforms with business services. Wisper is a mixed fixed-wireless and fiber operator. Treating all five as homogeneous fiber footprints would overstate owned fiber and understate integration or subsidy constraints. [S06,S09,S10,S11,S12,S13,S14,S15,S17]; recommended sequence: 1. Open a statewide route-diversity and IRU discussion with Sho-Me, focused on Springfield, Joplin, Jefferson City, Columbia, Rolla, Poplar Bluff and Cape Girardeau paths.; 2. Test a Bluebird commercial combination before any M&A thesis: reciprocal off-net access, protected waves, dark fiber, Springfield data-center connectivity, and Missouri NTIA-route interconnection.; 3. Maintain a sponsor-level Socket dialogue around future combination, market swaps or wholesale access, but do not underwrite a near-term bolt-on while Fastwyre is integrating and the 500,000-home target is being funded.; 4. Approach Kingdom as a cooperative partnership: backhaul, managed core, construction support or joint bids. Avoid assuming a sale perimeter.; 5. Use Wisper, Gateway and i3 as targeted product or geography discussions. Wisper is relevant for rural backhaul and selected fiber clusters; Gateway for eastern-Missouri FTTH and E-Rate enterprise; i3 for St. Louis and southeast-Missouri enterprise access after the T-Mobile deal status clears.
