Each offers local density near counties Omni says it plans to enter, but all require basic diligence on passings, subscribers, fiber title, capital needs and beneficial ownership before a transaction thesis is credible.

id: F3; type: public_fact; finding: Armstrong is the only screened fresh independent with clearly disclosed multi-state scale: the company says its family-owned network reaches more than 400,000 homes across six states. It completed and activated 970 fiber miles for more than 44,000 homes and businesses in southern Butler County on 2025-01-10. This is completed construction, not a subscriber count.

id: F4; type: public_fact; finding: FastBridge and Loop are not standalone fresh targets. Greenlight closed FastBridge on 2026-07-06 and completed Loop integration on 2026-07-23. Greenlight remains Oak Hill-backed; T-Mobile's announced 50/50 joint venture with Oak Hill is expected to close in the first half of 2027, so it is pending rather than current ownership.

id: F5; type: public_fact_and_inference; finding: Tri-Co Connections is the strongest co-op alternative, not an M&A target. By its 2025 annual meeting, all Tri-County REC members had access, almost 3,000 fiber miles were complete and more than 8,500 members were connected. Its practical role is public-private deployment, wholesale or financing partnership, and a rural operating benchmark.

id: F6; type: public_fact; finding: Pennsylvania's 2026 provisional BEAD list awards Armstrong Cable 3,425 fiber locations and $19.9 million, Advanced Telephone 12 fiber locations and $17,229, and VitaLink 188 fiber locations and $1.73 million. The statewide summary does not identify counties. Advanced Telephone appears with Hickory/Aurora in Washington County's project award. QCOL's site carries a VitaLink copyright and links to a VitaLink careers page, suggesting affiliation, but the reviewed sources do not establish that the VitaLink award belongs inside QCOL's legal perimeter.
gaps: No public passings, subscribers, revenue, EBITDA or fiber-mile totals were located for Hickory, QCOL or Salsgiver. Unknown is retained rather than estimated.
Beneficial ownership and exact affiliate perimeters remain unverified for Hickory/Advanced Telephone, QCOL/VitaLink and Salsgiver Inc./Salsgiver Telecom.
The statewide 2026 BEAD approval summary does not allocate Armstrong, Advanced Telephone or VitaLink awards by county, and provisional locations are not completed passings.
Citizens is an announced extension. Final transfer approval and legal closing remain unresolved; its D25 filer stays separate from Omni.
The atlas supplies a separate dated FCC availability baseline. Company-reported scale, current construction stages and exact route or location overlap are distinct evidence classes.

regionalResearch.title: Michigan
findings: type: public_fact; finding: 123NET is not an independent Michigan target for Rightfiber. Grain acquired a 65% controlling interest in 123NET in July 2024, with carryover owners retaining 35% at closing, and Grain completed the Ritter Communications and Great Plains Communications combination into Rightfiber on September 2, 2026.

type: analytical_inference; finding: The cleanest Rightfiber Michigan route is an internal Grain portfolio strategy around 123NET, then selective partnerships or tuck-ins. For Omni, D&P is the most geographically immediate independent conversation because its Lenawee and western Monroe network directly meets Omni's Monroe, Lambertville, Temperance and Milan build cluster.

type: public_fact; finding: PFN is a carrier, transport, public-sector and NG911 infrastructure provider, not a demonstrated mass-market FTTH platform. Its 6,400 route miles and statewide NG911 role must not be read as 6,400 retail fiber miles or statewide residential availability.

type: public_fact; finding: Michigan's approved BEAD final-proposal data allocates locations to 123NET, Surf, MEC and Cherry Capital, but these are awards or proposed obligations, not completed passings. The statewide totals shown are 19,332 for 123NET, 17,627 for Surf, 10,617 for MEC, 3,915 for Cherry Capital and 19 for Southwest Michigan Communications, the legal name used in public records for part of the Bloomingdale platform.

type: screen_out; finding: Great Lakes Energy's Truestream is a credible operating benchmark but was not elevated into the seven-company list. It is available only to GLE electric members, had more than 28,700 connected members as of December 18, 2025, and is cooperative-owned, making a wholesale or co-build discussion more realistic than a control transaction.
gaps: Current cap tables are unknown for D&P, PFN, Bloomingdale's related entities and Cherry Capital. Sponsor absence is not asserted where no current ownership filing was found.
Michigan-only passings and subscriber counts are not disclosed for Surf. Its 200,000 actual passings and 330,000 target are three-state figures.
D&P disclosed no project-specific 2025-2026 construction scale. Bloomingdale disclosed no current total passings or subscribers.
The Michigan BEAD final-proposal PDF is an award/allocation source. It does not establish acceptance of every location, construction start, completion, or current availability.
No valuation, revenue or EBITDA estimates were made where compatible primary-source inputs were unavailable.
The atlas supplies a separate dated FCC availability baseline. Company-reported scale, current construction stages and exact route or location overlap are distinct evidence classes.

regionalResearch.title: Ohio
findings: id: F01; classification: public_fact_plus_inference; finding: Omni faces the densest direct overlap from Armstrong and MCTV in Stark, Wayne, Medina, and Mahoning-area markets, from Buckeye in Toledo and Erie County, and from Bascom around Tiffin and Fostoria. Omni's current service page lists Massillon, Wooster, Medina, Poland, Toledo, Sandusky, Tiffin, and Fostoria at some stage of availability or construction. This makes these operators execution benchmarks and local competitive threats, not merely a theoretical buyer universe.

id: F02; classification: public_fact_plus_inference; finding: altafiber and Shentel are the clearest scaled carrier alternatives. As of February 17, 2026, altafiber reported fiber available to 70,000 residential and business addresses in the Dayton region of Ohio. Its $200 million and 2,300-route-mile figures describe the completed Dayton-build target, not the current 70,000-address actual. As of June 30, 2026, Shentel reported 475,677 Glo Fiber expansion-market passings and 19,847 total fiber route miles across its multi-state perimeter; those figures are not Ohio-only. Neither company is evidenced as available for sale. Their scale weakens a scarcity claim for Omni but also identifies credible future strategic counterparties.

id: F03; classification: public_fact_plus_reconciliation; finding: Armstrong announced a definitive agreement to acquire MCTV on February 17, 2026, with an expected second-quarter 2026 close. Current MCTV and Armstrong pages say MCTV is now Armstrong and describe a customer transition, but no explicit closing release or closing date was found. Treat MCTV as a transitioning transaction perimeter, not a separately available target and not a confirmed closed transaction for valuation purposes.

id: F04; classification: public_fact_plus_inference; finding: Bascom and NKTelco demonstrate that local Ohio fiber value can reside in governance structures that constrain a simple sale. Bascom describes itself as the area's only locally headquartered telecommunications cooperative, while NKTelco has been part of family-owned Schurz Communications since 2021. Partnership, network lease, wholesale access, or selective asset arrangements are therefore more defensible routes than assuming whole-company availability.

id: F05; classification: analytical_inference; finding: The strongest Omni carrier pitch is not that Ohio lacks fiber competitors. It is that Omni can offer a single newer FTTH operating platform across many smaller markets while the competitive landscape is fragmented among a large sponsor-owned ILEC, a public super-regional carrier, family-owned cable operators, a cooperative, and a family-owned broadband portfolio. Any pitch should show address-level overlap, duplication risk, and actual subscriber economics before assigning a scarcity premium.
gaps: Armstrong and MCTV's public sites indicate transition, but no explicit transaction closing release or closing date was found. Purchase price and transferred legal entities are also undisclosed.
Armstrong's current Ohio FTTH passing count and Buckeye's current total FTTH passing count were not found in primary sources.
Bascom's scheduled 2026-06-30 Phase 1 completion was not independently confirmed. Glo Fiber's Lancaster second-half 2025 completion target was not independently reconciled to a later city count.
No operator was tested for household income, and no income conclusion is made. No current sell-side availability is assumed for any company.
The atlas supplies a separate dated FCC availability baseline. Company-reported scale, current construction stages and exact route or location overlap are distinct evidence classes.

regionalResearch.title: Colorado Arizona
findings: id: F1; classification: [Inference] strategic conclusion; finding: Only Ting presents a disclosed near-term transaction catalyst. Tucows continued a strategic review of Ting through August 6, 2026, explicitly including asset sales, partnerships and other strategic transactions. Maverix is the best smaller independent to monitor, but its expansion is grant-defined and dispersed. ALLO, Wyyerd and Wecom are funded growth platforms; Highline is an acquisitive operator; Pulse is municipal and is not an ordinary M&A target.

id: F2; classification: public fact and [Inference] combination logic; finding: The cleanest regional combination concepts are Ting's Colorado assets with a Colorado consolidator, Highline plus Maverix for a broader rural Colorado footprint, and Wyyerd plus the remaining Simply Bits operation for Southern Arizona density. The latter is not a pure FTTP combination because Simply Bits' current retail product is fixed wireless. A Wyyerd-Wecom tie-up could create metro-plus-rural Arizona coverage, but it would be a large sponsor-to-sponsor transaction between two growth platforms, not a practical RightFiber add-on.

id: F3; classification: public fact; finding: Municipal broadband must be treated as partnership infrastructure, not conventional acquisition inventory. Loveland owns Pulse; Timnath funds construction while Pulse owns and operates the network under an intergovernmental agreement. Longmont's NextLight and Fort Collins Connexion are also community-owned systems. Their relevant routes are operating agreements, transport, wholesale, intergovernmental arrangements or selected asset-use rights.

id: F4; classification: public fact; finding: Operator-versus-contractor tests passed for all seven names. Highline is the operator even though Atlantic Engineering Group has been a construction partner and part-owner. ALLO uses contractors but owns or operates service networks; in Yuma County, the county owns the middle-mile network and ALLO operates and markets it. Wecom is the ISP; eX2 is the state middle-mile conduit operator in a separate access arrangement. None of those contractors should be counted as an additional retail operator.

id: F5; classification: [Inference] RightFiber fit; finding: Every screened asset is outside RightFiber's current core geography. Even the best regional targets are therefore lower-priority than contiguous or in-core opportunities. Ting merits event-driven monitoring, while Maverix merits a relationship and grant-compliance screen. The other five are watchlist names for capital markets, partnership or counterparty intelligence rather than priority RightFiber combinations.
gaps: Current cap tables for Highline and Maverix were not disclosed in accessible primary sources. ALLO's post-June 2025 SDC percentage was also not found.

Colorado's broadband site blocked several page fetches. Accessible state or local government documents confirmed key Maverix awards and first connections, but a primary current construction status for every Chaffee, Saguache, Gilpin and Boulder segment was not available.
Wyyerd does not publicly disclose Arizona passings, subscribers, revenue or route miles in the reviewed sources.
Wecom's 2025 CPF report extended AZ-EXTEND to April 15, 2026, but no primary closeout confirming final completion was located.
Ting does not disclose Colorado-specific passings, subscribers or EBITDA. Simply Bits' current customers and coverage were not updated from the 2021 acquisition figures.
The atlas supplies a separate dated FCC availability baseline. Company-reported scale, current construction stages and exact route or location overlap are distinct evidence classes.

regionalResearch.title: Carolinas Refresh
findings: Ripple is under a signed July 2026 Eaton acquisition agreement, with closing unverified. Platform Investment Partners and KLT are disclosed continuing shareholders. The pending transaction supersedes an independent control-target thesis.

TruVista is a sponsor-backed platform screen; Comporium is a long-held private operator with attractive regional density. Public evidence does not establish a sale process or willingness to transact for either.
Lumos is a T-Mobile / EQT wholesale joint venture. Segra is an enterprise and carrier network. Neither should be treated as a straightforward independent residential bolt-on.

RiverStreet, SkyLine/SkyBest and Sandhill require cooperative and project-specific structuring. West Piedmont’s termination of RiverStreet is a specific Virginia project event, not evidence of a companywide exit.

Unknown: TruVista's current sponsor ownership percentage and timing for any exit remain unknown.

regionalResearch.title: Virginia Refresh
findings: status: public_fact; claim: Virginia is already segmented among a 50/50 T-Mobile-EQT wholesale joint venture, a public integrated carrier, sponsor-backed rural builder, two cooperative structures, an active multi-state consolidator and a local private builder. This is not a blank-space statewide entry market.

status: analytical_inference; claim: All Points Broadband and ZiTEL are the two most actionable Virginia counterparties. All Points offers a sponsor dialogue and utility-partnership operating model; ZiTEL offers a local operating or capital-partnership route after replacing RiverStreet on the West Piedmont project. Neither is proven to be for sale.

status: public_fact; claim: The Lumos transaction closed on April 1, 2025. T-Mobile invested $932 million for 50% of the joint venture and approximately 97,000 fiber customers; EQT Infrastructure VI owns the other 50%. T-Mobile is the anchor tenant and owns residential and small-business customer relationships while Lumos operates as a wholesale network platform.

status: public_fact; claim: Point Broadband and Clearwave closed their combination on May 4, 2026. Their September 8, 2026 Visionary agreement was signed but had not been reported closed as of the screen date.

status: public_fact; claim: The West Piedmont commission replaced RiverStreet with ZiTEL on August 5, 2026 after RiverStreet could not secure remaining project capital. ZiTEL is scheduled to complete 14,161 connections across Franklin, Henry and Patrick counties by year-end 2027.

status: analytical_inference; claim: RightFiber has the stronger geographic logic for Southwest Virginia because its current residential footprint includes Tennessee and Kentucky. Omni Fiber currently markets service only in Ohio, Pennsylvania, Michigan and Texas, making a Virginia retail move noncontiguous. Point is the best geographic fit for RightFiber but is an active consolidator, not an available tuck-in; ZiTEL is the more actionable local relationship after delivery proof.
gaps: The DHCD annual report is current only through grantee monthly reports ending August 2025. Later company and county updates supersede it only for the specifically cited milestones.
ZiTEL's ultimate equity ownership and current subscriber count were not found in primary public sources.

The West Piedmont commission states a 14,161-connection ZiTEL project target, while a ZiTEL release cited approximately 14,547 potential customer locations. The government figure is used because the perimeter difference was not reconciled.
RiverStreet's post-August 2026 status was not fully reconciled for every East, Dinwiddie and separate Virginia grant project. The West Piedmont termination is not treated as a statewide exit.
All Points does not publish a current companywide FTTH passing or subscriber count. County grant targets were not summed into a corporate footprint because perimeters and completion dates differ.
Point-Clearwave's Visionary agreement was announced on September 8, 2026. No primary source confirming closing was found as of September 20, 2026.

regionalResearch.title: Enterprise Platforms
findings: Conclusion: none of the three is an easy bolt-on. Uniti is a public, nationwide operating company with $10.65 billion of notes and other debt at 2026-06-30. FirstLight is a mature, sponsor-owned Northeast platform. SummitIG is a sponsor-backed, data-center dark-fiber specialist that completed an acquisition in 2026 and is still expanding.

Best near-term route is commercial before corporate: test a route-specific wholesale, IRU, wavelength, resale, or joint-build arrangement against actual customer demand. A corporate transaction should follow only after a location-level network overlay, asset-title review, contract and concentration diligence, and evidence that the owner is willing to transact.

Uniti offers the broadest product and geographic reach and has publicly discussed monetizing non-core assets, but has not identified these three buyers, any relevant assets, or a sale process. FirstLight offers a coherent Northeast extension, but its published network-mile figures conflict. SummitIG offers the densest data-center thesis, but public financial and customer-concentration data are absent.

No reviewed primary company, SEC, or fund source accessible through 2026-09-20 announced a current sale process for Uniti, FirstLight, or SummitIG. That negative search result is not evidence that no confidential process exists. No availability is inferred.
gaps: No location-level GIS, building, POP, or route overlay against RightFiber or Great Plains was performed. No geographic overlap is claimed.
FirstLight's current public materials conflict between 20,000 and 25,000 route miles. No primary reconciliation was found.

Owned-versus-leased miles are not quantitatively disclosed for Uniti or FirstLight. SummitIG calls its network fully owned, operated, and maintained, but does not publish a route-level title, conduit, ROW, or IRU schedule.

FirstLight and SummitIG do not publish current revenue, EBITDA, debt, liquidity, capex, customer-concentration, churn, or contract-backlog data. Uniti does not publish segment top-customer concentration or a numerical data-center count.
No current sale process was announced in the reviewed accessible primary sources. A confidential process cannot be ruled out and is not inferred.
Current ownership percentages for SummitIG minority investors are not publicly restated after the 2021 Harrison Street transaction.
The atlas supplies a separate dated FCC availability baseline. Company-reported scale, current construction stages and exact route or location overlap are distinct evidence classes.

LiveOak is InfraRed-supported, Wire3 is majority-owned by Oak Hill, and IQFiber is SDC-backed. Sponsor identity changes the approach; financing announcements do not establish seller willingness.

atlas.methodology: Technology50 FTTP; residential-capable R/X; location_id deduplicated per filer within measured states. These are reported availability locations as of December 31, 2025, not passings, subscribers or proof of construction. Filer totals must not be summed into unique regional coverage. Legal filers are historical reporting identities, not necessarily current independent operators. Retained D25 input revisions vary: Carolina provider extracts precede the latest state-file revision. The newer-vintage probe was inconclusive; this is a dated D25 baseline, not a claim of the latest available release.
atlas.ownershipMethod: Original FCC legal-filer identities are retained. Selected current-control notes are dated overlays. Unannotated filers have not received a current ownership review; no automatic acquisition union is applied.

acceleratedAnalyses.title: Brightspeed: reconcile FCC availability with the build story
acceleratedAnalyses.summary: The full 20-state filing count is 1.79 million residential-capable FTTP locations. Brightspeed separately reported more than 3 million fiber-enabled locations in April 2026. Geography explains part of the original shortfall; the remaining definitions still need an address-level bridge.
acceleratedAnalyses.scope: Public research as of September 20, 2026. FCC availability as of December 31, 2025; current retained file revision September 15, 2026. Company figures are dated reported measures, not audited equivalence to FCC locations.
